new.title: Find a 1286 monstrance at Het Stadsmus
new.desc: Hasselt's city museum fills two joined town houses, the Waerdenhof of 1680 and the Stellingwerff house of 1857. Its star piece is a monstrance ordered in Paris in 1286 for Herkenrode Abbey, thought to be the oldest in the world, shown alongside Hasselt silver and the colourful ceramics the town made between 1895 and 1954.
new.tip: Guided climbs of the carillon tower run on the first Saturday of the month, so ask at the desk if you want the view as well.

new.title: Look up at Het Sweert on the Grote Markt
new.desc: The half-timbered corner house at Grote Markt 3 was first recorded as an inn in 1462 and got its present look in 1659. Its sign shows a sword held in an armoured fist, an old apothecary symbol, and fittingly the house has been a pharmacy since 1713.
new.tip: Stand on the Kapelstraat corner to see how the top floor juts out over the street, with St Andrew's crosses set between the timbers.

new.title: Buy the Hasselt praline at Chocoladehuis Boon
new.desc: Hasselt has its own praline, and Chocoladehuis Boon in the pedestrian centre is the only place that sells it. Patrick Mertens and Inge Lijnen opened the house in 2005, and Mertens has since been named Chocolatier of the Year.
new.tip: Ask about the pralines flavoured like Limburgse vlaai too. A small box travels better than a slice of the real thing.

new.title: Pull up a stool at volkscafé Cambrinus
new.desc: Cambrinus has officially been pouring beer since 1870 and is counted as an institution of Hasselt café life. The interior is said to have gone unchanged for some eighty years, and the crowd runs from eighteen to eighty.
new.tip: This is a place for a plain pils and a chat at the bar, not for cocktails. It sits in Het Dorp, the lively street just north of the Grote Markt.

new.title: Work through twelve taps at De HopHemel
new.desc: De HopHemel started as a brewery without a home and now runs its own taproom near Hasselt station. Twelve craft beers come fresh from the tap, with a small menu and a food pairing that changes every month.
new.tip: The taproom opens from mid afternoon, Wednesday to Saturday. Sunday openings are announced on its social media.

new.title: Fill a basket with Limburg flavours at Lekker Limburgs
new.desc: This shop gathers the food and drink of the whole province under one roof: fruit syrups, knapkoek from the Maasland, spelt jenever, local cheeses and wines from Limburg vineyards. It is the easy way to taste the region without driving round it.
new.tip: It closes on Sunday and Monday and over lunch, and some days it opens only in the afternoon, so check the hours first.

new.title: Do the morning market on Kolonel Dusartplein
new.desc: Twice a week the big square on the east side of the centre fills with market stalls, a habit that carries on even on most public holidays. Trading runs on Tuesday and Friday from about eight until half past twelve.
new.tip: Come before ten for the best choice. The city has plans to move one of the two market days to another spot, so check which square is in use.

new.title: Skate or sprawl in Kapermolenpark
new.desc: Hasselt's green lung lies along the Demer between the centre and the Japanese Garden, on ground where sand dug out for the Albert Canal was dumped in the 1930s. It has a pond, a playground, a jogging track and one of the largest open-air skateparks in the Benelux.
new.tip: On Thursdays in the summer holidays the Kaperconcerten take over the event square. In November the park hosts an international cyclocross race.

new.title: Let the kids loose at Plopsa Indoor Hasselt
new.desc: Belgium's first largely indoor theme park opened on Christmas Eve 2005 next to the arena at Park H. Around two dozen gentle rides, from bumper cars to a small coaster, are themed on Studio 100 characters such as Bumba, Maya and K3.
new.tip: It is aimed at toddlers and primary school children. Dated tickets bought online are cheaper than open ones.

new.title: Puzzle over the dodecahedron in the Gallo-Roman Museum
new.desc: Tongeren began as the Roman town of Atuatuca Tungrorum, and this museum tells the region's story from the Neanderthals to the early Middle Ages. Look for the Celtic gold, the Roman glass and the bronze dodecahedron whose purpose nobody has managed to explain.
new.tip: The museum is closed on Mondays. The reconstructed faces of Roman-era locals in the entrance hall can be seen without a ticket.

new.title: Follow the Roman wall to the Moerenpoort
new.desc: The Moerenpoort is the last of Tongeren's six medieval gates, first built between 1257 and 1264 on the remains of the Roman wall and rebuilt from 1379 after an attack. Beside it runs a long stretch of the original second-century Roman rampart.
new.tip: Walk through the gate into the beguinage quarter behind it. The name comes from the marshes that once lay outside the walls.

new.title: See the painted church of the Sint-Truiden beguinage
new.desc: The Sint-Agnes beguinage was founded in the mid-13th century and once housed more than 200 beguines. Its church, begun in 1258, is the oldest beguinage church in Flanders, with medieval wall paintings that were rediscovered in 1860 and an organ of 1646 that may be the oldest playable one in Belgium.
new.tip: The beguinage is open to walk through by day. The church now serves as a hall for exhibitions and concerts, so it is open when something is on.

new.title: Wander Koen Vanmechelen's Labiomista in Genk
new.desc: On the site of the old Zwartberg coal mine, later a private zoo, artist Koen Vanmechelen has built a 24 hectare open-air artwork. Swiss architect Mario Botta designed its two main buildings, and the grounds are shared by the artist's crossbred chickens, llamas, emus, dromedaries and storks.
new.tip: The park opens from spring to autumn and is closed on Mondays. Last entry is in the late afternoon but you may stay on until early evening.

new.title: Drink a Tripel Kanunnik in the barn at Wilderen
new.desc: A farm brewery since 1743 and a jenever distillery since 1890, Wilderen fell silent in 1939 and lay derelict until a couple rebuilt it and reopened in 2011. Today the half-timbered barn is a busy café for the house beers and spirits, and the old distillery with its steam engines can be visited.
new.tip: No reservations are taken for the café and it fills up on sunny weekends. Hours are shorter in winter, so check before cycling out.

new.title: Taste abbey beer at the castle brewery of Ter Dolen
new.desc: Brewer's daughter Mieke Desplenter bought the ruined 16th-century moated castle De Dool in 1990 and spent four years restoring it. Since 1994 Ter Dolen abbey beers have been brewed in the farm buildings, and they are poured on the terrace in the castle grounds.
new.tip: A light-hearted brewery tour of about 45 minutes runs on Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays in mid afternoon. It is in Dutch and should be booked online.

new.title: Walk the woods and watch the stars at Kattevennen
new.desc: Kattevennen is the Genk gateway to the Hoge Kempen national park and its theme is space. Signposted loops of 5 to 12 km start at the door, a path of some thirty stones lays out 500 million years of geology, and the Cosmodrome planetarium runs shows for all ages.
new.tip: From October to March there is stargazing on Saturday evenings when the sky is clear. You can walk here from Genk station through Molenvijverpark.

new.title: Climb the spoil heaps at Terhills in Maasmechelen
new.desc: Where the Eisden coal mine worked until 1987, the main gateway to the Hoge Kempen national park is now a landscape of wooded spoil heaps and lakes. Three of the four heaps can be climbed for wide views over the Maas valley, and a 380 metre bridge for walkers and cyclists runs between them.
new.tip: The red walk of about 9.5 km from the visitor centre is the one the park itself recommends. Entry to the walking area is free and there is a mine-themed playground by the terrace.
new.q: National Park Visitor Center Terhills, Zetellaan 54, Maasmechelen
